Progressive
pruh-GRESS-iv
adjective; noun (weaponized word)
Of multiple origins, partly from French progressif and partly from Latin progressivus, per the Oxford English Dictionary, which records its earliest evidence from around 1450, in Richard of Wallingford’s Exafrenon, an astronomical sense. The OED lists political and religious uses from the 1830s.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Progressive first meant moving forward or advancing step by step, as a heavenly body moves along its course; the OED’s earliest sense is astronomical, about 1450. It later took on senses in medicine, commerce, education and grammar, and from the 1830s in politics and religion, for those favouring change and reform. In American history the Progressive Era ran from about the 1890s to World War I or the Great Depression, and its reform movement was to a significant extent rooted in and energized by religion; the contemporary progressive movement is largely secular by comparison. The Christian observation: progress is a good word if it has a fixed destination. “The path of the just is as the shining light, that shineth more and more unto the perfect day” (Pro 4:18). But the LORD also commands, “Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein” (Jer 6:16), and “Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set” (Pro 22:28). Paul warned of those “Ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth” (2Ti 3:7).

Webster 1828 Definition

Advancing step by step (OED, about 1450); in politics from the 1830s, favouring change and reform. A label that claims the future and casts opponents as backward. True progress shines more and more unto the perfect day (Pro 4:18).

expand to see more

PROGRESSIVE, adj. and n. (from about 1450, OED) 1. Moving forward; advancing by stages. 2. (Politics, from the 1830s) Favouring change, reform or innovation; a person who does. From French progressif and Latin progressivus.

History note: the American Progressive Era, about the 1890s to 1917 or 1929, was to a significant extent religiously motivated; the contemporary movement is largely secular (Wikipedia, “Progressivism in the United States”).

Key Scripture

Pro 4:18 — "But the path of the just is as the shining light, that shineth more and more unto the perfect day."

Jer 6:16 — "Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein."

Pro 22:28 — "Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set."

2Ti 3:7 — "Ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth."

Modern Corruption

Progressive claims the future for one side: change is assumed to be advance, so the old paths are cast as backward without being shown false.

expand to see more

Progress means getting closer to a goal. A movement that names itself progressive without naming the goal has made change itself the measure, and anyone who resists the change is cast as standing in the way of the future. The word wins the argument by its grammar before a reason is given.

Scripture has a fixed destination, the perfect day of Pro 4:18, and it measures progress by nearness to it. Sometimes progress means going forward; sometimes it means turning back to the old paths that Israel refused (Jer 6:16). A people ever learning and never coming to the truth (2Ti 3:7) is not progressing at all, however fast it moves.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin progressivus / French progressif → progressive (OED about 1450, astronomy) → politics and religion (1830s) → Progressive Era (1890s–) → secular movement label.
